newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: British diplomats looking for PNG mercenary leader.
newsitem.headline: British diplomats looking for PNG mercenary leader.

text.p: British diplomats said on Wednesday they were trying to track down a former United Nations peacekeeper leading a group of mercenaries hired to put down an island uprising in Papua New Guinea.

Brian Baldwin, Britain's Deputy High Commissioner in the South Pacific Nation, told Reuters the High Commission was trying to reach Colonel Tim Spicer, chief executive of British-based Sandline International, and a colleague.
Baldwin said he believed Spicer and another former British officer were being held by rebel army officers in a barracks on the outskirts of the South Pacific nation's capital.
"We've been trying to find out exactly where he is and how he is but we've been able to make no contact at all, though we've tried many times," Baldwin told Reuters by telephone.
British newspaper reports say Spicer is a former colonel in the Scots Guards with 20 years' experience in the Falklands, Cyprus, the Gulf and Northern Ireland.
He was miltary attache to General Sir Michael Rose, the former commander of U.N. peacekeeping forces in Bosnia, and was quoted around the world as a U.N. military spokesman in besieged Sarajevo.

Spicer arrived in Papua New Guinea last month, leading a group of 40 mercenaries, mostly South African. Their arrival drew international criticism -- and infuriated PNG troops already frustrated at their poor equipment and pay.
Baldwin said Sandline had not been able to reach Spicer since Wednesday and had asked Britain's diplomats in Port Moresby for help.
"They (Sandline) have been in touch with us several times over the last 24 hours asking us to try and find out what the situation is," he said.
Baldwin believed Spicer was being detained by troops loyal to sacked Papua New Guinea Defence Force (PNGDF) chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok.

Singirok was dismissed by Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan on Monday after demanding Chan's resignation and the cancellation of PNG's US$28 million contract with Sandline. But he has not left his Port Moresby headquarters and officers from all ranks on Thursday demanded that Chan reinstate him.
"He's in one of the barracks in Port Moresby. As far as we know it's officers who are still loyal to the former commander who are detaining him," Baldwin said.
"We haven't been able to make contact with anybody. We're planning on trying to make contact and it's a bit difficult at the moment...who to make contact with."
Six of the 40 mercenaries left Papua New Guinea late on Wednesday, telling reporters on a stopover in Singapore that Sandline's contract had been terminated.
